claim: Magnetogenetics is a technique where thermo-sensitive and mechano-sensitive ion channels are genetically engineered to be closely coupled to the iron-storage protein ferritin.
source: This is the approach of a recent technique development, commonly termed magnetogenetics, where thermo-sensitive and mechano-sensitive ion channels are genetically engineered to be closely coupled to the iron-storage protein ferritin (Stanley et al., 2012; Stanley et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2016; Wheeler et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work on magnetogenetics.

claim: The plausibility of magnetogenetics has been challenged on physical grounds.
source: The plausibility of presented mechanisms of mechanical and thermal activation of ion channels has been challenged on physical grounds (Meister, 2016), and the present state of reported experimental observations in magnetogenetics and basic magnetic physics arguments that challenge those observations remain in conflict.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Meister (2016) who challenged the physical plausibility.

claim: Assigning magnetic moment values to iron atoms is highly variable and chemistry dependent.
source: Assigning the magnetic moment value to the iron atom between 0μB to 5μB (where μB is the Bohr magneton, μB = 9.27x10−24 Am2) and spin coupling configuration (paramagnetic, ferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic, antiferromagnetic, etc.) is highly variable and chemistry dependent (Coey, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Coey (2010) on magnetic properties of iron.

claim: The systematic and complete analysis of magnetism of the iron loaded ferritin core in magnetogenetics articles has not been performed.
source: It should also be pointed out that the systematic and complete analysis of magnetism of the iron loaded ferritin core in all the reported magneto-genetics articles has not been performed, and therefore the magnetism of the fundamental magneto- genetic ferritin construct is not presently known.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's assessment of the existing literature on magnetogenetics.

claim: Iron forms different mineral forms within ferritin, such as magnetite Fe3O4 or maghemite ɣFe2O3.
source: It is generally believed that iron forms different mineral forms within ferritin (for example, magnetite Fe3O4 or maghemite ɣFe2O3).
evidence: The claim is based on general scientific knowledge about iron mineralization in ferritin.

claim: The L*H chimera ferritin construct exhibited significantly enhanced iron loading ability.
source: The original enhanced iron-loading chimeric ferritin, reported by Iordanova et al. (2010) was characterized only by NMR and MRI, and showed that one of the fused heavy H and light L subunits constructs (the L*H chimera) exhibited significantly enhanced iron loading ability.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Iordanova et al. (2010).

claim: The maximum possible number of iron atoms in ferritin is N = 4500.
source: In my analysis, I use the commonly stated maximum possible number of iron atoms in ferritin N = 4500 and assume atomic moment of mFe = 5μB per iron atom (the highest value reported for iron in oxide form, Table 3.5 in Coey, 2010), with the understanding that the actual number of iron atoms in ferritin in all the magnetogenetics reports is not presently known.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chasteen and Harrison (1999) and Coey (2010).

claim: For the superparamagnetic spin arrangement, the particle magnetic moment at 1 Tesla is m = 2×10−19 (Am2), three orders of magnitude higher than for the paramagnetic state.
source: However, for the superparamagnetic (Figure 2c) spin arrangement (n = 1, black curve of Figure 3a), the particle moment saturates at relatively low magnetic fields, well below 1 Tesla, where the magnetic moment has the value of m = 2×10−19 (Am2), three orders of magnitude higher than for the paramagnetic state.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The assumption about spin configurations of iron atoms in ferritin has dramatic effects on the total magnetism of the particle.
source: It is immediately apparent that the assumption about the spin configurations of iron atoms in the ferritin protein has dramatic effects on the total magnetism of the particle.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis and calculations presented in Figure 3a.

claim: Most experimental reports on ferritin magnetism indicate paramagnetic particles.
source: Most experimental reports on ferritin magnetism indicate paramagnetic particles (Meister, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Meister (2016).

claim: There have been experimental reports on iron-loaded ferritin where the magnetization measurement closely follows the superparamagnetic curve.
source: In fact, there have been experimental reports on iron-loaded ferritin where the magnetization measurement closely follows the superparamagnetic curve (black line in Figure 3a) (Bulte et al., 1994; Moskowitz et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bulte et al. (1994) and Moskowitz et al. (1997).

claim: The saturation magnetic moment of a superparamagnetic particle of N = 4500 iron atoms with moments of 5μB per atom is mTOT = 22500 μB = 2.1 x 10−19 (Am2).
source: In the present analysis, the saturation magnetic moment of a superparamagnetic particle of N = 4500 iron atoms with moments of 5μB per atom is mTOT = 22500 μB = 2.1 x 10−19 (Am2), consistent with the numbers reported in experiments by Bulte et al. (1994) and Moskowitz et al. (1997), suggesting that the superparamagnetic state of iron-loaded ferritin might be possible.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations and comparison with experimental data from Bulte et al. (1994) and Moskowitz et al. (1997).

claim: The saturation magnetization MS of the 8 nm diameter ferritin particle is MS = 7.8×105 (A/m).
source: It is also instructive to consider the saturation magnetization, MS, of magnetite in my calculation by dividing the particle saturation moment mTOT by the volume V of the 8 nm diameter particle (MS = mTOT/V) which results in MS = 7.8×105 (A/m).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using the particle volume and saturation moment.

claim: Commonly reported bulk magnetite magnetization is MS = 4.8×105 (A/m).
source: Commonly reported bulk magnetite magnetization is slightly lower at MS = 4.8×105 (A/m) (Coey, 2010), but it should be noted that several reports (Arora et al., 2008; Orna J et al., 2010; Guan et al., 2016) indicate that magnetite magnetization increases significantly in the size range below 10 nm and reaches the value of MS = 1×106 (A/m).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coey (2010) and other studies on magnetite magnetization.

claim: The force from an externally applied magnetic field gradient on iron loaded ferritin, even the superparamagnetic one, is too low to be effective for ion channel activation.
source: This confirms that the force from an externally applied magnetic field gradient on iron loaded ferritin, even the superparamagnetic one, is too low to be effective (Meister, 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on force calculations and comparison with required forces for ion channel activation, with citation to Meister (2016).

claim: The minimum required force to mechanically activate ion channels is on the order of 1 (pN) = 10−12 (N).
source: The minimum required force to mechanically activate ion channels (Milo and Phillips, 2016) is on the order of 1 (pN) = 10−12 (N).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Milo and Phillips (2016).

claim: The maximum possible force between two superparamagnetic ferritin particles is on the order of F = 10−10 (N) = 100 (pN), well above the required level for activating an ion channel.
source: Such a large magnetic field gradient from one ferritin particle acting on the second ferritin particle (and therefore on the mechanosensitive ion channels coupled to the ferritin particles) results in the maximum possible force on the order of F = 10−10 (N) = 100 (pN), well above the required level for activating an ion channel.
evidence: The claim is based on force calculations between two ferritin particles.

claim: If the ferritin construct is superparamagnetic, there is theoretical plausibility that two ferritin particles pulling on each other could result in sufficient force to activate mechano-sensitive ion channels.
source: Therefore, if the construct reported by Iordanova et al. (2010) and used by the magnetogenetics reports is similar in its magnetism or even more enhanced than what was reported by other superparamagnetic ferritin results of Bulte et al. (1994) and Moskowitz et al. (1997), then there is at least the theoretical plausibility that the two ferritin particles pulling on each other could result in a sufficient force to activate mechano-sensitive ion channels to which the ferritin particles are coupled.
evidence: The claim is based on force calculations and comparison with experimental data, involving inference about theoretical plausibility.

claim: For modest clustering of N = 4500 iron spins into n = 450 clusters of N/n = 10 exchange coupled spins each, the interaction energy of the particle rises above kBT level in a field of 1 Tesla.
source: However, it is interesting that even for modest clustering of N = 4500 iron spins into say n = 450 clusters of N/n = 10 exchange coupled spins each (n = 450 dark blue curve in the plot) the interaction energy of the particle rises above kBT level in a field of 1 Tesla.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations shown in Figure 3b.

claim: There is in principle a theoretical possibility that an external magnetic field can exert sufficient torque on an anisotropic ferritin particle (on the order of 10−19 N·m in a 1 Tesla external field) to activate mechano-sensitive ion channels.
source: Therefore, there is in principle a theoretical possibility that an external magnetic field can exert a sufficient torque on an anisotropic ferritin particle (on the order of 10−19 N·m in a 1 Tesla external field) to activate mechano-sensitive ion channels.
evidence: The claim is based on torque calculations and involves speculation about theoretical possibility.

claim: Diamagnetism can have dramatic mechanical effects on biological materials, such as levitation or restriction of water flow, if large magnetic fields and field gradients are simultaneously present.
source: Diamagnetism is generally considered the weakest form of known magnetism (Coey, 2010; Yamaguchi and Tanimoto, 2006), but it can have surprising and dramatic mechanical effects on biological materials (most of which are diamagnetic), such as levitation (Geim et al., 1999; Simon and Geim, 2000) or restriction of water flow (Ueno and Iwasaka, 1994a; Ueno and Iwasaka, 1994b), if the conditions of large magnetic fields and field gradients are simultaneously present.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies on diamagnetic effects.

claim: The combination of magnetic fields and field gradients from the ferritin particle results in the critical parameter B∇B = 8.1x10^8 (T^2/m), many orders of magnitude larger than anything available in common laboratory settings.
source: This results in the critical parameter in the diamagnetic force calculations of B∇B = 8.1x108 (T2/m), many orders of magnitude larger than anything available in the common laboratory settings (Simon and Geim, 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations and comparison with laboratory conditions, with citation to Simon and Geim (2000).

claim: Neural cells have extremely low Young's modulus, E, on the order of E = 100 (Pa), the lowest of any known materials.
source: The consensus that is emerging from the studies of mechanical properties of ion channels and cell membranes (Lu et al., 2006; Sánchez et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2018) is that neural cells have extremely low Young's modulus, E, on the order of E = 100 (Pa), the lowest of any known materials.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on mechanical properties of neural cells.

claim: The diamagnetic susceptibility of ion channels and cell membranes is similar to that of water, on the order of χ = -1x10−5.
source: It is reasonable to assume that this number is similar to that of water (Coey, 2010), on the order of χ = -1x10−5, but one should not dismiss the possibility that ordered lipid cell membrane domains could have an order of magnitude higher value of diamagnetic susceptibility (Braganza et al., 1984; Ginzburg et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with water and citations to studies on lipid membrane diamagnetism.

claim: The estimated cell membrane deformation due to diamagnetic force is d = 0.4 nm = 4 Å.
source: Combining Equation (5) with Equation (6), using the listed parameters, and assuming for simplicity that the diamagnetic force (of Equation (5)) is applied uniformly only across 1 nm of cell membrane thickness (due to the sharp drop of fields and field gradients from the magnetite particle), results in the deformation distance d = 0.4 nm = 4 Å.
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using contact mechanics equations.

claim: An Angstrom-scale deformation represents a significant fractional change of the overall cell membrane thickness and is known to be sufficient to affect ion channel behavior.
source: This is of course only a crude estimation, but such an Angstrom-scale deformation represents a significant fractional change of the overall cell membrane thickness, and is known to be sufficient to affect ion channel behavior (Tyler, 2012; Hamill and Martinac, 2001; Reeves et al., 2008) and is also quite likely to do so in mechano-sensitive magnetogenetics constructs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on ion channel mechanosensitivity.

claim: Magneto-caloric effect refers to the heating and cooling of magnetic materials by DC magnetic fields.
source: Magneto-caloric effect refers to the heating and cooling of magnetic materials by DC magnetic fields (Coey, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Coey (2010).

claim: Magnetic adiabatic cooling has been used in low-temperature physics to obtain milliKelvin temperatures in paramagnetic salt powders and sub-milliKelvin temperatures with nuclear spins in metals.
source: This process of magnetic adiabatic cooling has been used in low-temperature physics for a long time (Giauque, 1927) to obtain milliKelvin temperatures in paramagnetic salt powders and sub-milliKelvin temperatures with nuclear spins in metals (Simon, 1952).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Giauque (1927) and Simon (1952).

claim: Magnetic adiabatic energy transfer can be potentially performed at higher temperatures if the spins are segregated and coupled into superparamagnetic clusters.
source: Although such magnetic adiabatic energy transfers are generally performed only at cryogenic temperatures, McMichael et al. (1992) have pointed out that this process can be potentially performed at higher temperatures if the spins are segregated and coupled into superparamagnetic clusters (such as shown in the spin configuration of Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McMichael et al. (1992).

claim: For a given magnetic field B and temperature T, there is an optimal clusterparamagnetic size that will generate maximum entropy change and energy transfer from the spin ensemble to the magnetite particle lattice.
source: For a given magnetic field B and temperature T, there is an optimal clusterparamagnetic size that will generate maximum entropy change and energy transfer from the spin ensemble to the magnetite particle lattice (McMichael et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McMichael et al. (1992).

claim: The hypothesis that optimal clusterparamagnetic size generates maximum entropy change has been experimentally confirmed.
source: This hypothesis seems to have been experimentally confirmed (McMichael et al., 1993; Shao et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McMichael et al. (1993) and Shao et al. (1996).

claim: For magnetic field change of 1 Tesla, the ferritin particle with N = 4500 iron spins that separate into n = 15 equal clusters of N/n = 300 exchange coupled spins in each cluster will provide the maximum energy transfer to the magnetite particle lattice.
source: For magnetic field change of 1 Tesla (black points in Figure 6), the ferritin particle with N = 4500 iron spins that separate into n = 15 equal clusters of N/n = 300 exchange coupled spins in each cluster will provide the maximum energy transfer to the magnetite particle lattice.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations shown in Figure 6.

claim: For the paramagnetic spin state of the ferritin particle, no value of magnetic field is sufficient to achieve magneto-caloric particle energy change near the level of kBT.
source: For the paramagnetic spin state of the ferritin particle (N = n = 4500 point in Figure 6) no value of magnetic field is sufficient to achieve magneto-caloric particle energy change near the level of kBT.
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations shown in Figure 6.

claim: If N = 4500 iron spins cluster into n = 100 (or fewer) clusters of N/n exchange coupled spins each, the magneto-caloric energy transfer from the spin ensemble to the magnetite particle lattice is higher than the kBT level.
source: However, if N = 4500 iron spins conceivably cluster into n = 100 (or fewer) clusters of N/n exchange coupled spins each, the magneto-caloric energy transfer from the spin ensemble to the magnetite particle lattice is higher than the kBT level, including for the superparamagnetic state (n = 1 point in Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations shown in Figure 6.

claim: It is not clear how magneto-caloric energy transfer from the clusterparamagnetic spin ensemble to the thermo-sensitive or mechano-sensitive ion channel could occur for channel activation, but the energy scales indicate it is theoretically feasible.
source: It is not clear how this magneto-caloric energy transfer from the clusterparamagnetic spin ensemble of the magnetite particle to the thermo-sensitive or mechano-sensitive ion channel could occur for channel activation, but the energy scales in the magneto-caloric process indicate that it is theoretically feasible.
evidence: The claim is based on energy scale calculations and involves speculation about feasibility.

claim: A large number of iron-loaded ferritin particles expressed throughout the neural cell membrane may generate a global temperature rise that is orders of magnitude larger than the negligible short timescale temperature rise adjacent to a single iron-loaded ferritin protein.
source: However, it may also be that a large number of iron-loaded ferritin particles expressed throughout the neural cell membrane generate a global temperature rise (on a longer timescale) that is orders of magnitude larger than the negligible short timescale temperature rise adjacent to a single iron-loaded ferritin protein (Zheltikov, 2018; Keblinski et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citations to Zheltikov (2018) and Keblinski et al. (2006).

claim: Magnetic moment m of a particle is proportional to mechanical angular momentum L of that particle, m = ɣ·L, where ɣ is the gyromagnetic ratio.
source: It is a fundamental tenet of quantum mechanics that magnetic moment m of a particle is proportional to mechanical angular momentum L of that particle, m = ɣ·L, where ɣ is the gyromagnetic ratio, ɣ = e/me, for spin angular momentum of iron (where e is charge of the electron and me is mass of the electron [Coey, 2010]).
evidence: The claim is based on fundamental quantum mechanics principles with citation to Coey (2010).

claim: The Einstein-de Haas effect refers to the magneto-mechanical effect where a reversal of a magnetic moment of a sample by an applied magnetic field has to be accompanied by a corresponding change in mechanical angular momentum of that sample.
source: The Einstein-de Haas effect refers to the magneto-mechanical effect, required by the conservation of angular momentum, where a reversal of a magnetic moment of a sample by an applied magnetic field has to be accompanied by a corresponding change in mechanical angular momentum of that sample.
evidence: The claim is based on fundamental physics principles.

claim: The Einstein-de Haas effect has been experimentally confirmed on both the macroscopic and microscopic samples, and recently also on the molecular scale.
source: This physical principle has been experimentally confirmed on both the macroscopic (Scott, 1962) and microscopic samples (Wallis et al., 2006), and recently also on the molecular scale (Ganzhorn et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Rotational kinetic energy of 0.33x10−21 (J) by a single magnetite particle moment reversal is a significant fraction of kBT = 4.28x10−21 (J).
source: Rotational kinetic energy of 0.33x10−21 (J) by a single magnetite particle moment reversal (one half of the applied AC magnetic field cycle) is a significant fraction of kBT = 4.28x10−21 (J).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of calculated energy with thermal energy.

claim: The maximum energy loss per cycle typically reported for magnetic hyperthermia applications is 1 (J/kg).
source: It is interesting to compare this value to the maximum energy loss per cycle of 1 (J/kg) typically reported for magnetic hyperthermia applications (Hergt et al., 1998; Hergt et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hergt et al. (1998) and Hergt et al. (2006).

claim: The Einstein-de Haas effect should be considered on par with the typical Brown and Néel relaxation modes in magnetic particle hyperthermia in contributing to sample heating.
source: Therefore, it would appear that the Einstein-de Haas effect should be considered on par with the typical Brown and Néel relaxation modes in magnetic particle hyperthermia (Rosensweig, 2002; Dutz and Hergt, 2013; Deatsch and Evans, 2014) in contributing to the sample heating.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of energy values and citations to hyperthermia literature.

claim: The energy scale of the Einstein-de Haas torque is on the same order of magnitude as kBT = 4.28x10−21 (J).
source: The energy scale of this torque is again on the same order of magnitude as kBT = 4.28x10−21 (J).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of calculated torque energy with thermal energy.

claim: For the potentially superparamagnetic spin arrangement of the ferritin particle, the magnetic field near the particle surface is not static, but is fluctuating rapidly in time.
source: As described earlier, for the potentially superparamagnetic spin arrangement (Figure 2c) of the ferritin particle, the magnetic field near the particle surface (Figure 4a) has a relatively large value of 0.65 Tesla. This magnetic field from the particle is not static, but is in fact fluctuating rapidly in time (Brown, 1963; Brown, 1979), as I show schematically in Figure 8a.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brown (1963) and Brown (1979) on magnetic moment fluctuations.

claim: The frequency of superparamagnetic moment fluctuation at physiological temperature is in the GHz frequency range.
source: The frequency of this fluctuation at physiological temperature is significant and measured to be in the GHz frequency range through low-frequency magnetic susceptibility, Mossbauer spectroscopy, and neutron spin-echo spectroscopy (Kilcoyne and Cywinski, 1995; Allen et al., 2000; Casalta et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental measurements.

claim: Superparamagnetic moment fluctuations have been experimentally observed on a single particle scale at low temperatures.
source: Such superparamagnetic moment fluctuations have also been experimentally observed on a single particle scale at low temperatures (Wernsdorfer et al., 1997; Piotrowski et al., 2014; Hevroni et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: The ion channel in the vicinity of potentially superparamagnetic iron-loaded ferritin experiences large magnetic field gradients and Tesla-scale magnetic fields at GHz frequencies.
source: Therefore, the ion channel in the vicinity of the potentially superparamagnetic iron-loaded ferritin experiences large magnetic field gradients and Tesla-scale magnetic fields at GHz frequencies, as well as the corresponding GHz frequency diamagnetic forces and torques, as discussed earlier.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the fluctuating magnetic moment and previous calculations.

claim: There are no experimental or theoretical studies that have investigated cell membrane or ion channel behavior in conditions of combined high amplitude magnetic fields (Tesla-scale) and field gradients (10^8–10^9 T/m scale) and ultra-high frequencies (1–10 GHz scale).
source: I am presently not aware of any experimental or theoretical studies that have investigated cell membrane or ion channel behavior in such extreme conditions of combined high amplitude magnetic fields (Tesla-scale) and field gradients (108–109 T/m scale) and ultra-high frequencies (1–10 GHz scale), and yet that would appear to be the environment in which the genetically engineered ion channels in magnetogenetics might be operating.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's assessment of the literature.

claim: Many parameters critical to the full understanding of magnetogenetics remain unknown, including the exact iron magnetism, spin clustering configuration, spin dynamics, and magnetic anisotropy of the ferritin construct.
source: Many parameters that are critical to the full understanding of magnetogenetics remain unknown and include: (1) the exact iron magnetism, spin clustering configuration, spin dynamics, and magnetic anisotropy of the ferritin construct utilized so far in magnetogenetics studies, (2) the realistic mechanical and thermal nano-environment around the iron-loaded ferritin, (3) the diamagnetic (and perhaps even paramagnetic) properties of ion channels and cell membranes next to the iron-loaded ferritin, and (4) the functional properties of ion channels under the influence of simultaneously large amplitude and ultra-high-frequency magnetic fields and field gradients.
evidence: The claim is based on the author's assessment of what is known and unknown in the field.

claim: Modern techniques of SQUID and cantilever force and torque magnetometry have achieved spectacular magnetic moment sensitivities down to a single Bohr magneton.
source: In addition to the mentioned scanning probe methods and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and crystallography that are already being performed on a single ferritin particle level, modern techniques of SQUID (Cleuziou et al., 2006; Vasyukov et al., 2013) and cantilever force and torque magnetometry (Stipe et al., 2001; Tao et al., 2016) have achieved spectacular magnetic moment sensitivities (down to a single Bohr magneton).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on magnetometry techniques.

claim: Additional magnetic effects on ion channels in neural cell membranes could include phase changes and deformations in lipid bilayers due to magnetic fields.
source: It is entirely possible that additional magnetic effects on ion channels in neural cell membranes, such as the phase changes and deformations in lipid bilayers due to magnetic fields (Yamaguchi and Tanimoto, 2006; Maret and Dransfeld, 1977; Tenforde and Liburdy, 1988; Kurashima et al., 2002), gradient magnetic field effects on the ion diffusion (Kinouchi et al., 1988) and the resting membrane potential of cells (Zablotskii et al., 2016), as well as the induction of calcium influx in cells by nanomagnetic forces (Tay et al., 2016) could further influence magnetogenetic activation of cells.
evidence: The claim is based on citations to various studies on magnetic effects on biological systems.

claim: External DC and AC magnetic fields easily penetrate biological tissue.
source: This is mainly due to the fact that external DC and AC magnetic fields easily penetrate biological tissue, are easily generated by current carrying wires or permanent magnets, and their properties and engineering design tools are well understood.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about magnetic field properties.

claim: Magnetic fields are commonly used in medical diagnostics applications such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).
source: These features of magnetic fields are commonly used in medical diagnostics applications such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) (McRobbie et al., 2017), and there is a strong impetus to apply the same advantages of magnetic fields to control biological function, as is the case in Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) (Walsh and Cowey, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to MRI and TMS literature.

claim: Thermo-sensitive or mechano-sensitive ion channels of the TRP family (TRPV1 and TRPV4) were genetically engineered to be closely coupled to the novel chimeric iron-loading protein ferritin in magnetogenetics.
source: Thermo-sensitive or mechano-sensitive ion channels of the TRP family of channels (TRPV1 and TRPV4) were genetically engineered to be closely coupled to the novel chimeric iron-loading protein ferritin.
evidence: The claim is based on description of the magnetogenetics construct from the original articles.

claim: The criticism against magnetogenetics is fundamentally based on assumptions about the number of iron atoms (N = 2400) in the ferritin protein and the magnetic configuration that assumes iron spins as a collection of independent non-interacting particles (paramagnetic configuration).
source: This criticism is fundamentally based on the assumptions on the number of iron atoms (N = 2400) in the ferritin protein and on the magnetic configuration in ferritin protein that assumes iron spins as a collection of independent non-interacting particles (paramagnetic configuration).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of Meister's (2016) criticism.

claim: The physical viability of magnetogenetics depends critically on many physical parameters of the basic control construct that are presently not well known or understood.
source: Here, I present the case that the physical viability of magnetogenetics depends critically on many physical parameters of the basic control construct (iron-loaded ferritin protein coupled to the thermo-sensitive or mechano-sensitive ion channel in the cell membrane) that are presently not well known or understood, and therefore the physical possibility of magnetogenetics cannot yet be discounted and needs to be further explored.
evidence: The claim is the author's main argument based on analysis of unknown parameters.

claim: The physical possibility of magnetogenetics cannot yet be discounted and needs to be further explored.
source: Here, I present the case that the physical viability of magnetogenetics depends critically on many physical parameters of the basic control construct (iron-loaded ferritin protein coupled to the thermo-sensitive or mechano-sensitive ion channel in the cell membrane) that are presently not well known or understood, and therefore the physical possibility of magnetogenetics cannot yet be discounted and needs to be further explored.
evidence: The claim is the author's conclusion based on the analysis presented.

claim: The total energy of a spin system has terms related to the interaction of individual spins with the external magnetic field, plus the interaction energy of the spins among themselves.
source: The total energy of a spin system has terms related to the interaction of the individual spins with the external magnetic field, plus the interaction energy of the spins among themselves.
evidence: The claim is based on fundamental physics principles of magnetic systems.

claim: For interacting spin systems, the thermal energy may be too small to appreciably dephase the spins.
source: This total energy must be compared with the thermal energy and, for interacting systems, the thermal energy may be too small to appreciably dephase the spins.
evidence: The claim is based on fundamental physics principles of magnetic systems.

claim: The possibility for experimenters to exploit the interaction of magnetic nanoparticles in vivo with external magnetic fields (~1T) is not unreasonable.
source: Thus the possibility for experimenters to exploit the interaction of magnetic nanoparticles in vivo with external magnetic fields (~1T) is not unreasonable.
evidence: The claim is the author's conclusion based on consideration of spin interaction energies.

claim: Figure 1 shows thermo-sensitive or mechano-sensitive ion channel closely coupled to iron-loading protein ferritin with external DC or AC magnetic fields applied.
source: The fundamental genetically engineered construct in magnetogenetics, as reported by the original articles (Stanley et al., 2012; Stanley et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2016; Wheeler et al., 2016), is shown diagrammatically in Figure 1.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 1.

claim: Figure 2 shows three distinct spin coupling configurations of iron atoms in ferritin: paramagnetic, clusterparamagnetic, and superparamagnetic states.
source: Figure 2 diagrammatically shows the three distinct spin coupling configurations of iron atoms in ferritin that I consider as reasonable possibilities.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 2.

claim: Figure 3a shows ferritin particle magnetic moment vs. magnetic field as a function of different cluster numbers.
source: Figure 3a shows the resulting ferritin particle magnetic moment vs. magnetic field at T = 310K as a function of different cluster numbers and for the experimentally attainable laboratory magnetic fields (0 to 2 Tesla) generated by either electro-magnets, superconducting magnets, or permanent magnets.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 3a.

claim: Figure 3b shows the interaction energy magnitude (E = m·B) of the iron loaded ferritin as a function of the external magnetic field.
source: Figure 3b shows the interaction energy magnitude (E=m·B) of the iron loaded ferritin configurations of Figure 2 in the external magnetic fields between 0 and 2 Tesla.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 3b.

claim: Figure 4 shows diamagnetic ion channel in the cell membrane experiencing magnetic fields from the ferritin particle and externally applied magnetic field, resulting in repulsive diamagnetic force.
source: I suggest that this diamagnetic repulsive force might be sufficient to mechanically deform the ion channel and affect its function, as I diagrammatically describe in Figure 4.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 4.

claim: Figure 5 shows the basic magneto-caloric process where clusterparamagnetic moments change from high entropy state in zero field to low entropy state in applied field.
source: Figure 5 diagrammatically shows the basic process.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 5.

claim: Figure 6 shows magneto-caloric energy change as a function of the number of clusters n in the particle for different applied magnetic fields.
source: Figure 6 shows the numerical calculation results for that magneto-caloric energy change as a function of the number of clusters n in the particle.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 6.

claim: Figure 7 shows the Einstein-de Haas principle where magnetic moment reversal results in change of angular momentum compensated by mechanical rotation or torque on the particle.
source: Figure 7 shows schematically the basic Einstein-de Haas principle.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 7.

claim: Figure 8 shows that in zero external magnetic field, the ion channel experiences fluctuating Tesla-scale magnetic fields at GHz frequencies from the superparamagnetic particle, while in external field the ion channel experiences DC Tesla-scale fields.
source: Therefore, the ion channel in the vicinity of the potentially superparamagnetic iron-loaded ferritin experiences large magnetic field gradients and Tesla-scale magnetic fields at GHz frequencies, as well as the corresponding GHz frequency diamagnetic forces and torques, as discussed earlier. Upon application of the external DC magnetic field, of say 1 Tesla, the magnetic moment saturates, and the ion channel experiences DC magnetic field, field gradient, diamagnetic force, and torque, as I show in Figure 8b.
evidence: The claim describes the content of Figure 8.
